newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tax bill drops education item after veto threat.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tax bill drops education item after veto threat.

text.p: An education tax break provision aimed at parents with children in elementary and high schools was dropped from tax legislation after President Clinton threatened a veto over it, lawmakers said Wednesday.
Republican legislators released a letter from Clinton to House Speaker Newt Gingrich that they said was delivered about 10 p.m. EDT Tuesday.

At issue was a proposal by Sen. Paul Coverdell, a Georgia Republican, which would have allowed parents to contribute to an education account, similar to an Individual Retirement Account, aimed at saving money for the child's education from kindergarten through college.

"As you know, in working out the final agreement, I strongly opposed the Coverdell amendment," Clinton wrote in the letter dated July 29. "I would veto any tax package that would undermine public education by providing tax benefits for private and parochial school expenses," the letter said.

Congressional Republicans and the White House earlier this week reached agreement on a five-year $94 billion net tax cut package. But some details were still being nailed down and Congress is scheduled to vote on the bill Thursday.
Coverdell said after the letter threatening a veto was delivered, his proposal was dropped from the bill.
"I don't believe any of us would have the whole (tax bill) go down with it," Coverdell said, adding that his proposal would be resurrected at some later time.

The Coverdell proposal would have allowed parents to put $2,000 a year after-tax for each child into the education account. The interest earned on that money would be tax-free if used for the child's education.
